Records · history · technique

Pi Memorization Record

The Guinness world record for reciting the digits of π from memory is 70,030 digits, set by Suresh Kumar Sharma of India in 2015. Here's the full record book — plus how the champions actually do it, and how you can start.

The current record

On 21 October 2015, Suresh Kumar Sharma, a vegetable vendor from Jaipur, India, recited 70,030 digits of π without error. The recitation took 17 hours and 14 minutes, with short breaks every hour for food and bathroom visits. Guinness World Records officials, judges and a panel of independent observers verified each digit against a printed reference. Sharma had been preparing for six years.

He broke the previous official record of 70,000 digits, set earlier the same year by his countryman Rajveer Meena.

The unofficial record (and why it isn't official)

The largest recitation ever claimed is by Akira Haraguchi of Japan, a retired engineer who in October 2006 recited 100,000 digits of π over a continuous 16-hour, 30-minute session at a public hall in Kisarazu, near Tokyo. He was 60 years old.

Haraguchi's feat is widely accepted in the mathematics community but has never appeared in the Guinness Book. Guinness requires that the recitation be filmed continuously, that every digit be checked against a master list by independent witnesses, and that the recitation be done under controlled conditions. Haraguchi's session was filmed and witnessed, but the documentation submitted didn't meet the Guinness verification standard. He had previously reached 83,431 digits in 2005, surpassing the official record at the time, with the same outcome.

For Haraguchi, pi memorization is a philosophical practice. He treats each digit as a syllable in a vast story — turning 0–9 into characters and assembling them into narratives that he replays in his head.

The full record book

An abbreviated history of recognised pi memorization records:

  • 2015 · Suresh Kumar Sharma (India) — 70,030 digits in 17h 14m. Current Guinness record.
  • 2015 · Rajveer Meena (India) — 70,000 digits in roughly 10 hours, while blindfolded. Held the record for about 8 months.
  • 2006 · Akira Haraguchi (Japan) — 100,000 digits in 16h 30m. Unofficial; not Guinness-verified.
  • 2005 · Akira Haraguchi (Japan) — 83,431 digits. Also unofficial.
  • 2005 · Lu Chao (China) — 67,890 digits in 24h 4m. The official Guinness record holder for ten years, until Meena.
  • 1987 · Hideaki Tomoyori (Japan) — 40,000 digits in 17h 21m. The long-standing record of the late 20th century.
  • 1981 · Rajan Mahadevan (India) — 31,811 digits.
  • 1978 · David Sanker (USA) — 10,000 digits, the first widely publicised five-figure recitation.
  • 1973 · Edward Gaughan (USA) — 1,111 digits, the first widely publicised four-figure recitation.
  • 1853 · William Shanks (UK) — calculated (not memorised) 707 digits, of which 527 were correct. Memorisation records would not catch up to his number for over a century.

How memorisers actually do it

Memorising tens of thousands of digits is not a feat of raw recall — it's a feat of encoding. Every record-holder uses some scheme to convert numbers into something the brain naturally remembers: a sound, a story, a place, an image.

The Major System

The most popular technique. Each digit 0–9 is mapped to a consonant sound; vowels are free. Digits become syllables, syllables become words, words become sentences. 3.14159 might encode as "meteor flies" with the right table.

The Memory Palace (method of loci)

The memoriser imagines walking through a familiar building or street. Each room or landmark is associated with a chunk of digits, often encoded as a vivid image. Recall = walking the route in the mind. This is the technique used by most Memory Sport competitors, including those who tackle pi.

Story-based encoding

Akira Haraguchi's method: assign each digit a syllable, then weave the syllables into a long narrative. The "story" of pi he uses includes religious imagery and characters that make the sequence emotionally meaningful — and therefore stickier.

Piems and chunking

For shorter targets, many people use piems — poems where each word's letter count encodes a digit. The classic "How I want a drink, alcoholic of course…" gets you to 14 digits without much effort. Plain chunking (grouping digits in fives or tens and reciting them rhythmically) is enough to take most people past the first 100 digits.

How far can you get?

Most adults can comfortably memorise 50–100 digits with about an hour of focused practice using chunking and rhythm — no special technique required. Getting to 1,000 digits takes weeks of daily review and usually some encoding scheme. Beyond 10,000 digits, you're committing to a multi-year project with structured retrieval drills, scheduled rehearsal, and tolerance for the long, slow re-laying of forgotten chunks.

If you want to find out where you stand:

  • Play Pi — The Game in the browser to see how far you get when you have to type each digit live.
  • Print our first 1,000 digits sheet to study from.
  • Browse the first 10,000 digits or the first million when you're ready to push past where the references stop.

Why memorise pi at all?

The practical answer: you don't need to. Fifteen digits of pi are enough to compute the circumference of the observable universe to within the width of a hydrogen atom. NASA uses just 15 digits for its interplanetary trajectories. Anyone reciting more than that is doing it for love — for the meditative effect of practice, for the small thrill of being able to do something almost no-one else can, and for the simple beauty of a number that never ends.

Or, as Akira Haraguchi himself put it: "What I'm doing is the same as climbing a mountain. People climb mountains not because they have to, but because the mountain is there."
